name: Ready-to-Resume Plan
summary: A short note you write just before an interruption, recording where the task stands and what the next step is, so your mind can let go of it.
explanation:
A ready-to-resume plan is a brief written plan you make when you have to leave a task before it is finished. You write down where you are and what is still open, plus the exact next step you will take when you come back.

The idea comes from Sophie Leroy and Theresa Glomb (2018). They looked at people who get interrupted and expect time pressure when they return to the interrupted task. Those people kept thinking about the unfinished task. They showed more attention residue, and they did worse on the interrupting task. When participants spent about a minute writing a ready-to-resume plan before switching, attention residue dropped and they did better on the interrupting task.

Why does it work? An unfinished task keeps pulling at your attention because your mind does not trust that you will pick it up again (see the Zeigarnik effect and open loops). Writing down the next step gives your mind that guarantee. It's the same mechanism as the plan-making effect. The plan also shortens the resumption lag when you come back, since the context you need is already on paper.

How do you apply it? Before you answer the call, join the meeting or end the day, write two or three lines in the task itself, in a scratch file or in a top of mind note. A simple format works: "I am at X. Next: Y. Watch out for Z." Keep it short. The habit has to stay cheap enough to do EVERY time. Hemingway's habit of stopping mid-sentence (the Hemingway bridge) and a daily shutdown ritual are close cousins of the same practice.

articles.title: Tasks Interrupted: How Anticipating Time Pressure on Resumption of an Interrupted Task Causes Attention Residue and Low Performance on Interrupting Tasks and How a "Ready-to-Resume" Plan Mitigates the Effects
